transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2026-01-15 15:00 PT
Duration: 48 minutes
Attendees: Maya (Redwood AE), Leo (Redwood SE), Ruth (Redwood Solutions), Dr. Priya Menon (HorizonLabs CTO), Carlos Ruiz (SRE), Aisha Bello (Platform Eng), Samir Desai (Product)

Summary: quick console walkthrough focused on request-level tracing, error triage flow, Request Playback demo and playbook for debugging production spikes. Customer shared recent incident where ~2% of requests had token-level latency spikes + occasional 500s when routing to quantized variants. Team discussed hosted vs dedicated routing, VPC egress, and audit log retention.

Topics: request inspector, trace waterfall, kv-cache hits, model fallbacks, playback + sampling, RBAC for ops, SOC2/KMS questions, next steps for POC.

Transcript body:
[00:00] Maya Patel: okay hi everyone, welcome, thanks for joining today. we wanted to run through the console request flows, primarily the request inspector and playback, and then build a simple debug playbook you folks can use when you see spikes.
[00:15] Dr. Priya Menon: thanks Maya. quick context — we had a production incident last week where certain prompts to our summarization pipeline had much higher latency. also some 500s during heavy load when we fell back to quantized model.
[00:28] Leo Zhang: yep, that's a good one to walk through. Carlos, can you summarize what the alert looked like?
[00:34] Carlos Ruiz: sure -- it was alerts from our SLO tracking, we saw tail latency jump from ~300ms to multiple seconds for about 2% of requests, CPU usage on the inference host was fine but token times appeared to spike, and then for a subset we saw 502/503s when requests routed to a different model variant.
[00:52] Maya Patel: okay so two axes — token-level latency spikes, and model fallback errors. both are observable in the Console; we'll show the Request Inspector for the first, and Request Playback for the second.
[01:05] Ruth Chang: small note — sometimes the transcript engine mislabels the model name, so you'll see 'redwood-slim' in the logs but that might be an alias for the quantized drop-in.
[01:18] Aisha Bello: that's actually true, our infra maps internal names so we had to crosswalk.
[01:23] Leo Zhang: alright sharing screen now — jumping into Console -> Requests. first panel shows the request timeline, you can filter by status, model, route id. I'll click into a failing request.
[01:40] [screen noise, clicks]
[01:45] Leo Zhang: here's an individual trace, top shows timeline: receive -> routing -> queue -> model-init -> generate -> postprocessing. notice the long generate bar around token 512, you can expand to see per-chunk timing.
[02:05] Carlos Ruiz: wait, generate looks long but why is model-init short?
[02:09] Leo Zhang: good catch. this indicates the model was hot (kv cache warm), but generation per-token slowed — often due to kernel scheduling or longer attention due to padding. can you share example prompts?
[02:23] Samir Desai: we have them in the doc; I'll paste a sample in the chat.
[02:27] [chat paste sound]
[02:30] Maya Patel: looking at the prompt, I see a mix of long system messages plus user context— that increases effective sequence length. two mitigations: prefix caching and suggested batch shaping to reduce per-token compute.
[02:45] Dr. Priya Menon: prefix caching — we thought that only applied to repeated prefixes across users? we don't have a lot of repeated prefixes.
[02:52] Leo Zhang: it's most useful when you have repeated system context or standard instructions. but Console also surfaces KV cache hit rate per route; even small reuse helps. for ad-hoc long contexts, we recommend trimming or chunking.
[03:10] Carlos Ruiz: what's the recommended TTL for KV cache? we don't want stale state.
[03:15] Leo Zhang: default is fairly short, a few minutes; you can tune by route. there's a cache TTL field in the route config.
[03:24] Aisha Bello: going back to the 502/503s — do those come from model variants timing out?
[03:29] Ruth Chang: often it's a routing fallback where primary model fails and we proxy to a quantized variant with different performance characteristics and sometimes the runtime returns a 5xx if the variant isn't compatible with a particular request (e.g., function calling hooks).
[03:44] Maya Patel: Leo, can you switch to the Playback tab and show a recorded session where a fallback happened?
[03:49] Leo Zhang: yep switching — Request Playback lets you replay the exact request to the same model variant or to a compatible variant. here's a recorded request from the incident window. I'll replay to the dedicated cluster first.
[04:06] [clicks]
[04:10] Leo Zhang: replaying now — you can see the timeline overlay of the original, and the replay. interesting — on replay to dedicated we don't see the 503, but token pacing is still a few seconds longer.
[04:25] Carlos Ruiz: so replay cleared the 503, maybe a transient infra issue?
[04:29] Leo Zhang: possibly, or the fallback path had an incompatibility. Playback's compare view shows differences in headers, model flags and kv cache header presence.
[04:41] Dr. Priya Menon: can Playback emulate VPC egress settings? our prod is in a VPC private deployment.
[04:49] Leo Zhang: for Private deployments, playback runs inside the same vpc if you enable the playback agent; for hosted, playback is sandboxed. we can run a host-side playback in your VPC during the POC.
[05:03] Maya Patel: note for compliance — playback logs are sanitized by default but you can toggle raw payload retention if you have the right role and we've signed a DPA.
[05:12] Samir Desai: good to know. on the error analysis side, how do we correlate application traces to request ids?
[05:19] Leo Zhang: each Console request has a request_id you can inject into your app logs. we also support trace export to your tracing system (e.g., jaeger or datadog) via the tracing hook.
[05:31] Carlos Ruiz: we use Datadog — is the trace format standard?
[05:34] Leo Zhang: we emit OTLP/Jaeger-compatible spans; you can correlate by request_id. I'll share the connector doc after.
[05:41] [slight interruption, background]
[05:45] Aisha Bello: another ops question — RBAC for the console: can we restrict playback to only SREs?
[05:51] Ruth Chang: yes; Console has role-based access controls per workspace and route. you can create a role that allows request-inspector view but disallows raw payload retention or playback.
[06:02] Dr. Priya Menon: and audit logs for who ran playback?
[06:05] Maya Patel: fully logged. playback starts, we create an audit entry with actor, request ids, time, and whether raw retention was enabled. all retained in the audit log export for the retention window you buy.
[06:18] Carlos Ruiz: how long are audit logs retained by default?
[06:21] Maya Patel: default 90 days, with add-on up to 3 years for enterprise.
[06:27] Samir Desai: question — when you suggested batch shaping earlier, is that something Redwood Optimize can recommend automatically?
[06:34] Leo Zhang: yes — Optimize analyzes seq length distribution and suggests optimal batch sizes, concurrency, and whether quantized variants are likely to save cost without hurting latency. it also gives simulated cost delta.
[06:45] Aisha Bello: do you have a recommended playbook we can follow when we see a spike?
[06:50] Maya Patel: yes — here's the short playbook: 1) identify request_id and route; 2) open Request Inspector and check KV hit rate + per-token times; 3) run Request Playback to reproduce; 4) compare to non-quantized variant; 5) if fallback errors, check model compatibility flags and function call constraints; 6) if token times are high, consider batch shaping or sequence trimming; 7) capture trace and export to datadog and create a ticket.
[07:17] Carlos Ruiz: can you show step 3 live on a sample?
[07:21] Leo Zhang: sure — picking a sample failing request from your incident window. replaying to both hosted and a warm dedicated cluster.
[07:34] [clicks, replay starts]
[07:41] Leo Zhang: hosted replay shows intermittent 503s at about 40% CPU on the worker that handled that shard. dedicated shows no 503, but latency is still elevated versus baseline.
[07:57] Dr. Priya Menon: interesting — so dedicated removes the 503 flakiness but doesn't fix per-token slowness.
[08:03] Leo Zhang: right — for per-token slowness we'd look at kernel selection and sequence length distribution. we can also try a different compilation profile — Optimize can recommend a kernel/quantization profile for that model.
[08:18] Maya Patel: one more tip — enable Request Sampling for the route to automatically capture one in N requests with full payload and stack for offline analysis; set sampling to low for production to avoid cost.
[08:32] Carlos Ruiz: what's the cost of full payload capture?
[08:35] Maya Patel: it's billed per request captured and stored; we'll include a ballpark in the pricing sheet.
[08:41] [small pause]
[08:45] Samir Desai: security — we need to ensure KMS usage for model keys and also HSM access for private deployments, can you confirm options?
[08:55] Ruth Chang: yes, Private supports customer-managed KMS/HSM integrations. we also support bring-your-own-key for hosted with additional contractual requirements.
[09:06] Dr. Priya Menon: ok that's important for our compliance team.
[09:09] Maya Patel: we'll include the KMS integration doc in the follow-ups.
[09:14] Carlos Ruiz: small nit — sometimes in traces the model name is abbreviated, making it hard to match with our catalog. any suggestion?
[09:21] Leo Zhang: we expose a model mapping table in the Console settings; you can upload your local model aliases so the Console shows the canonical name.
[09:30] Aisha Bello: on the playback compare view there's a column 'headers differ' — what headers matter for routing?
[09:36] Leo Zhang: common ones: route-id, kv-cache token, model-variant flag, and any custom routing header you use. differences there can change execution path.
[09:45] Samir Desai: can you annotate traces with our internal ticket id automatically?
[09:49] Leo Zhang: yes, we support custom metadata injection so you can pass x-internal-ticket-id and it shows up in request metadata and search.
[09:57] Carlos Ruiz: good. so, operationally, if we start a POC, what's the recommended minimal scope for the 2-week pilot?
[10:04] Maya Patel: typical pilot: integrate SDK or API for one critical route, enable Request Sampling, share a 48h sample workload for playback, run Optimize recommendations, and run a few regression prompts to validate output quality. we'll commit an SE to help create the playback harness.
[10:21] Dr. Priya Menon: timeline wise — our compliance review takes about two weeks, so POC kickoff could be Jan 22 if we clear compliance.
[10:29] Maya Patel: that aligns. we'll send SOC2 + network diagram and a PO checklist to help speed review.
[10:36] [brief cross-talk]
[10:41] Leo Zhang: quick demo note — you'll see 'kv-cache-hit-rate' metric per route, and the timeline has vertical ticks for model switches; that's useful to spot fallback frequency.
[10:52] Aisha Bello: can we export requests matching a filter to S3 for batch analysis?
[10:57] Ruth Chang: yes, Console supports export connectors to S3 and GCS. you can schedule daily exports or ad-hoc.
[11:05] Carlos Ruiz: perfect.
[11:07] Samir Desai: last Q — any known gotchas when replaying requests with streaming responses? we use streaming a lot.
[11:15] Leo Zhang: streaming replay is supported but the compare UX differs — we record chunk boundaries; if your client consumes differently (e.g., different token join timing) you'll see differences. for debugging latency, we recommend replaying with both streaming and non-streaming to compare.
[11:31] Maya Patel: ok wrapping up with a recap.
[11:34] Maya Patel: action items: Leo will run playback against a 24h sample and share screenshots and the token/time breakdowns; I'll send SOC2 and pricing; Horizon to upload sample failing traces; schedule POC kickoff.
[11:48] Dr. Priya Menon: sounds good, appreciate the detailed walkthrough.
[11:52] Carlos Ruiz: thanks everyone.
[11:55] Maya Patel: thanks all, we'll follow up in email with links.
[12:00] [meeting ends]

Notes about transcript: occasional mislabels (model alias), minor background audio, and short timestamps approximate real meeting flow.
